blogs.title: Beyond Ciminelli: How 'Pump-and-Dump' Schemes Survive the Right-to-Control Rejection via Fraudulent Inducement
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's crucial distinction between the discredited "right-to-control" theory rejected in *Ciminelli* and the surviving "fraudulent-inducement" theory affirmed in *Kousisis*. It examines how *United States v. Constantinescu* clarifies that prosecutors need not prove a deprivation of abstract economic information to secure a securities fraud conviction; rather, they must show that misrepresentations caused victims to part with tangible money or property. The piece explores the doctrinal shift back toward traditional property interests in white-collar crime.

blogs.title: Intent to Defraud Without Intent to Harm: The End of the 'Net Loss' Requirement in Securities Fraud
blogs.description: Focusing on the mens rea element of fraud, this article discusses the court's rejection of the argument that defendants lack criminal intent if they do not aim to leave their victims financially worse off. Drawing heavily on *Kousisis*, the post explains why a "pump-and-dump" scheme constitutes fraud even if victims receive securities of equivalent market value at the time of purchase. It argues that this ruling solidifies a precedent where the act of obtaining money through deception is sufficient for liability, regardless of whether the defendant intended to inflict net pecuniary loss on the investor.

blogs.title: Social Media Influence and Traditional Property: Resolving Tensions Between Digital Speech and Fraud Statutes
blogs.description: This post considers the broader implications of applying decades-old fraud doctrines to modern social media influencers. It addresses the tension between free speech concerns regarding financial advice online and the strictures of federal fraud laws. By analyzing how the Fifth Circuit treated social media posts as instruments of "fraudulent inducement" rather than mere informational exchanges, the article evaluates whether this decision expands federal reach into digital commentary or simply reaffirms that lies told to extract capital remain illegal regardless of the platform used.
